name: Zweigelt

lines.s10: Zweigelt is the juicy red of Austria: sour cherry and a pinch of black pepper, soft on the tongue and happy to be served cool.
lines.s20: Zweigelt is the red Austria pours every day, a crossing of two older local grapes made in 1922. It is juicy and soft, with sour cherry, raspberry and a little black pepper, and it likes a light chill.
lines.s45: Zweigelt is Austria's everyday red, grown from the banks of the Danube to the Hungarian border. It tastes of sour cherry and raspberry with a pinch of black pepper, and it is juicy and medium bodied, with fresh acidity and soft tannin. Most of it is made in steel tanks and sold young, while the fuller wines from around Lake Neusiedl rest in oak barrels and pick up a little vanilla. Pour it lightly chilled with schnitzel, sausages or roast chicken. It is a young grape, a crossing made near Vienna in 1922 from two older local reds, Blaufränkisch and Saint Laurent.
lines.sale: Zweigelt is the bottle for a guest who loves Pinot Noir and wants to try something new: much the same easy weight, with sour cherry and a peppery snap. I would pour it lightly chilled with roast chicken or anything fried.

glass.lead: Sour cherry and raspberry with a pinch of cracked black pepper, juicy and medium bodied, on fresh acidity and soft tannin.

ladder.where: Lower Austria: the Weinviertel and the Kamptal
Burgenland around Lake Neusiedl, and Carnuntum

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, tannin medium and soft, alcohol moderate, body medium.

home.home: Austria, where it is grown across the country's wine regions. The warm shore of Lake Neusiedl in Burgenland and the slopes of Carnuntum, east of Vienna, give the fullest wines, some of them aged in small oak barrels. Lower Austria's are lighter, made in steel and sold young. It is also pressed for rosé.
home.abroad: Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia grow it next door, mostly for light reds and rosé. Further off it has taken to cold places: the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia and Hokkaido in Japan.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius: lightly chilled, an oaked Reserve a little warmer.
service.glass: A plain red wine glass; a Burgundy bowl flatters a fuller, barrel aged bottle.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary: it is made to be opened and poured.
service.age: Young, within three or four years; a Reserve from Burgenland or Carnuntum keeps five to ten.

with.why: fresh acidity cuts the fried crumb

with.dish: Sausages, cold cuts and dark bread

labels.means: The grape's longer name on some Austrian labels: the same wine.
A second legal name for the same grape; a few growers prefer it, since the breeder was a National Socialist.
The lakeside origin in Burgenland whose red is Zweigelt; a Reserve blend holds at least 60 per cent.
The grape's name on Czech and Japanese labels: Zweigelt vine, nothing more.

guest.q: I usually drink Pinot Noir. Will I like this?
guest.a: I think so. It is a little darker and juicier, with sour cherry and a peppery snap where Pinot Noir has silk and forest floor, and it is just as easy with food.

guest.q: It smells so fruity. Is it sweet?
guest.a: No, it is dry. Ripe sour cherry and raspberry can read as sweetness on the nose, but there is no sugar left in the wine and the finish is fresh.

guest.q: How on earth do I say it?
guest.a: TSVYE-gelt. The Z is said as ts and the W as v, in two syllables with the weight on the first.

compare.tell: Blaufränkisch, its parent, is darker and firmer, with blackberry, more black pepper, higher acidity and real tannin; Zweigelt is softer, juicier and ready sooner.
Gamay is paler and lighter, with violet and often a candied banana note; Zweigelt is darker, with sour cherry, pepper and a touch more tannin.
Pinot Noir is paler and silkier, with forest floor under its red cherry; Zweigelt is purple at the rim, juicier and plainer, with a peppery finish.

profile.st: Ruby with a violet tint · Body medium · Acid medium to medium plus · Tannin medium and soft · Alcohol moderate
profile.fruit: Sour cherry, raspberry, redcurrant; black cherry and blackberry in the fuller wines of Burgenland and Carnuntum
profile.other: Cracked black pepper and a touch of liquorice; vanilla and cocoa where the wine has seen small oak barrels; mostly unoaked and sold young
profile.tell: Juicy sour cherry with a peppery snap, soft tannin and a violet tinted rim: darker than Gamay, softer than Blaufränkisch
profile.regions: Austria throughout: Neusiedlersee and Carnuntum for the fuller wines, Lower Austria for the lighter; Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia
profile.confuse: Blaufränkisch is darker, firmer and more peppery; Gamay is paler and lighter, often with banana; St Laurent is silkier and more perfumed

cards.front: Zweigelt: which two grapes were crossed, where, and in what year?
cards.back: Blaufränkisch and Saint Laurent, crossed by Fritz Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg, near Vienna, in 1922. Rotburger is its second legal name.

cards.front: Zweigelt: which lakeside Austrian origin is built on it?
cards.back: Neusiedlersee, in Burgenland, a protected origin since 2012. Its Reserve may be a blend, with at least 60 per cent Zweigelt.

cards.front: Zweigelt against Blaufränkisch in a blind glass: what parts them?
cards.back: Zweigelt is softer and juicier: sour cherry, medium tannin, made to drink young. Blaufränkisch is darker, with blackberry, more black pepper, higher acidity and firm tannin, and it keeps.

questions.q: An Austrian red poured blind is ruby with a violet tint, juicy and medium bodied, with sour cherry, raspberry and a pinch of black pepper, fresh acidity and soft tannin. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Juicy sour cherry, a little pepper and soft tannin point to Zweigelt. Blaufränkisch, its parent and the nearest wrong answer, is darker and firmer, with higher acidity and real grip.

questions.q: A guest reads Rotburger on an Austrian label and asks what grape that is. What do you tell her?
opts: Zweigelt, under its second legal name
Pinot Noir, as Austria names it
Saint Laurent, under an old name
questions.exp: Rotburger is a legal synonym for Zweigelt in Austria. Blaufränkisch is Lemberger in Germany, and Pinot Noir is Blauburgunder in Austria.

questions.q: A guest who enjoyed a light Zweigelt asks for a fuller one, from where the grape ripens most fully. Which Austrian origin do you look for on the list?
questions.exp: The warm shore of Lake Neusiedl is the origin built on Zweigelt and gives its fullest reds. The Wachau and Traisental are white wine country, and Weststeiermark is known for Schilcher rosé.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. A thin grape: the profile is written new, in the manner of the reviewed ones, and agrees with the Régionale row (acidity, body and tannin all medium; sour cherry and pepper; juicy).
The Régionale row calls Zweigelt the most planted red of Austria. The entry leaves that out as volatile and says the everyday red.

The year the grape took the name Zweigelt is left out: the sources disagree (1975 in a wine glossary and the press, 1978 in the Austrian ministry's page, which cites the federal gazette), and the common line that the breeder himself named it Rotburger is disputed. The entry says only that Rotburger is a second legal name.

The Rotburger label line states that the breeder was a National Socialist, which is why a few growers prefer the other name (the national wine body published a historian's study of it, and the press reported the renaming campaign of 2018). The owner may strike the clause; the line stands without it.

Abroad: Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia stand on the Codex's own Hungarian readings and two reference pages; the Okanagan Valley on British Columbia wines listed under the provincial quality mark; Hokkaido on the town of Yoichi's own winery page and a competition record. Ontario is left out for want of a second source.
Violet as a scent is left out: the national wine body speaks of a violet tint in the colour, not of a floral note.

Service follows the reference's row for light reds, and the national wine body's own campaign for serving its reds lightly chilled. No Creole dish is given: none of the seven truly suits better than the four listed.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open austrianwine.com directly (the host is outside the session's network). The checker should open the four addresses.
